facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: FICO's operations generate strong, growing cash flow, but the June 30, 2026 balance sheet is a different credit from the one at FY2025. In nine months, with total debt rising by US$2,526.7m, the company drew a new US$1,500.0m term loan, issued US$1,000.0m of 2034 notes, repaid the US$400.0m 2018 notes and borrowed further on the revolver, taking total debt from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m. The proceeds funded US$3,046.0m of share repurchases, including a US$1,500.0m accelerated share repurchase, far above free cash flow. On an analyst EBITDA of operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, total debt to EBITDA moved from 3.25x to 4.46x, and cash interest cover from 9.07x to 7.60x on a lagging cash-paid basis. Interest on the new debt is only partly in the last twelve months, so the run-rate burden is materially higher than reported cash interest. The main limits are the absence of a company-defined EBITDA or covenant ratio, the absence of the credit agreement, and the absence of anything after the July 29, 2026 filings. Of the term loan, US$300.0m falls due within twelve months. The base is sufficient to run the downstream modules with these limits stated.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: FICO is a Delaware-incorporated, NYSE-listed analytics company with two segments. Scores sells the FICO Score mainly through Experian, TransUnion and Equifax, which pay FICO a fee for each score generated; Software sells decisioning products as SaaS or on-premises. Revenue is concentrated by counterparty (three bureaus), by end market (financial services) and by geography (the Americas), and recent growth is concentrated in Scores pricing on mortgage originations. The company has no sponsor and no controlling holder is evidenced in the supplied sources; ownership detail sits in a proxy statement that is not supplied. The creditor-relevant change in the period is financial policy: in FY2026 the company issued new notes, drew a term loan and funded a large accelerated share repurchase, taking analyst total debt to EBITDA to 4.46x per the financial base. The documented behaviour is debt-funded shareholder distribution within the permissions of an unsecured credit agreement and in compliance with its stated covenants; no priming, drop-down or non-pro-rata exchange is documented. The business is high-margin and cash generative, but its revenue depends on a small number of counterparties and on score pricing, so the credit rests on continued pricing power and on management's leverage choices, not on structural protection.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: There is no sponsor transaction, merger or acquisition in the supplied sources; the context lists no deal terms. The transactions that matter to a creditor are the issuer's own financing and capital return events in fiscal 2026. On March 20, 2026 the company issued senior notes carrying a 6.25% coupon and maturing September 15, 2034, in a private offering to qualified institutional investors, and on March 26, 2026 it used the proceeds to repay in full the 2018 Senior Notes before their May 2026 maturity (10-Q page:12). On June 5, 2026 it amended its credit agreement to provide a term loan borrowed in full that day and maturing May 15, 2028, with quarterly amortisation, and the 10-Q states that the proceeds were used to fund an accelerated share repurchase agreement (10-Q page:11, page:22). The same day it entered an accelerated share repurchase agreement with Wells Fargo Securities, paying $1.5 billion and receiving an initial delivery of shares equal to approximately 80 percent of the expected total, with $300.0 million treated as a prepayment pending settlement, which the company expects in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 (10-Q page:13). The June 2026 repurchase program authorises repurchases up to an aggregate cost of $2.0 billion, of which $800.0 million remained at June 30, 2026, including the prepayment awaiting settlement (10-Q page:36). In sum, the financing replaced a maturing note with a longer note and added a term loan whose proceeds were returned to shareholders, taking total debt from US$3,055.7m at September 30, 2025 to US$5,582.4m at June 30, 2026 per the financial base. Liquidity effect: cash is US$248.4m and the derived undrawn revolver is US$290.0m before letters of credit, and the term loan amortises at a quarterly rate with US$300.0m due within twelve months. The status of each event is completed except the settlement of the repurchase agreement, which is a stated expectation, and the September 30, 2026 instalment and later events are Not supplied because nothing after the July 29, 2026 filings is in the pack. The credit agreement, its June 5, 2026 amendment, the indenture for the 2026 notes and the repurchase agreement are not supplied, so the amortisation schedule, guarantor position, covenant definitions and any restrictions on distributions rest on the 10-Q summary text. The use of proceeds and debt raised are Documentary Facts; the characterisation of the repurchase as returning capital to stockholders is Management Language (10-K page:63).

facts.label: Revenue durability
facts.text: - Evidence: bureau revenue was 63% of the June 2026 quarter (10-Q page:15) and the Scores segment growth was "primarily attributable to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price" (10-Q page:26). - Mechanic: a per-score fee through three intermediaries means a small number of contract terms and one pricing lever set revenue; Software is a smaller, slower segment. - Implication: revenue is durable while FICO Score use is required or preferred in mortgage and consumer credit decisions, but pricing and policy shifts can lower it quickly; a revenue shortfall hits debt service and the covenant ratio together. Counter: the retention rate above 100% in platform software (10-Q page:25) supports part of the base.

facts.label: Request
facts.text: - Issuer: FAIR ISAAC CORP (Fair Isaac Corporation, NYSE "FICO", issuer id fico), as of 2026-11-05, information cutoff 2026-11-05. - Scope: the fundamental credit view a committee reads first, synthesised from the settled upstream registers only: business risk from the business and transaction context, financial risk and liquidity from the financial base, and the gaps that limit both. Creditor perspective. - Prohibited and not done: no peer ranking, no instrument recommendation, no recovery conclusion. Recovery appears only as a mechanic where relevant. No rating is assigned. - Evidence rule: upstream only. This module re-read no source text and quotes nothing. facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: FICO's business risk is strong on earnings quality but narrow on sources: a per-score fee model with very high segment margins, recurring Software revenue with net retention above 100%, light capital spending and consistent free cash flow. Its financial risk has moved sharply in fiscal 2026. Total debt rose from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m while cash repurchases of US$3,046.0m for nine months far exceeded free cash flow of US$750.0m, and analyst total debt to EBITDA rose from 3.25x at FY2025 to 4.46x at June 30, 2026, which is 4.26x net. The stated covenant maximum is 4.5x until December 30, 2026, then 4.0x, then 3.5x, and on the analyst measure the cushion below 4.5x is thin; on a sensitivity that adds back share-based compensation the ratio is 3.91x. The covenant definition is not supplied, so headroom is Not calculable. Interest on the June 2026 debt is only partly in reported cash interest, so run-rate cover is about 3.96x against 7.60x reported. Liquidity is adequate for the near term but not generous: cash of US$248.4m plus a derived undrawn revolver of US$290.0m, against US$300.0m of term loan amortisation due within twelve months, which free cash flow comfortably covers. The next refinancing step is large: US$1,987.5m falls due in FY2028, when the term loan balance and the 2019 and 2021 notes mature. Because the debt is unsecured and no creditor-adverse action is documented, the creditor relies on covenants, cash generation and the board's financial policy, not on collateral or a sponsor. Overall the fundamental credit view is a high-quality earnings stream carrying a materially higher and still discretionary debt load; confidence is medium because covenant definitions, ownership detail and everything after July 29, 2026 are Not supplied.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The most important finding is that leverage is now set by shareholder-return policy rather than by operations. CP-1 shows total debt up from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m over nine months and nine-month cash repurchases of US$3,046.0m against free cash flow of US$750.0m; the business context shows the term loan proceeds were used to fund an accelerated share repurchase and that a $2.0 billion repurchase authorisation is in place. The mechanism is direct: each repurchase round is financed by borrowing, so analyst total debt to EBITDA of 4.46x can rise or fall by board decision alone. The implication is that the creditor's leverage tolerance depends on a choice nobody has committed to constrain, other than the financial covenant.

facts.text: The second finding is the covenant path. The stated maximum consolidated leverage ratio is 4.5x until December 30, 2026, 4.0x from December 31, 2026 and 3.5x from December 31, 2027. On the analyst measure of operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, total debt to EBITDA is 4.46x, which leaves a cushion of 0.95% of EBITDA below 4.5x (Calculations); on the sensitivity with share-based compensation added back it is 3.91x. The covenant definition is not supplied, so neither is the covenant ratio, and the compliance statement in the filings is the only evidence of headroom. The step down to 4.0x on December 31, 2026 requires EBITDA growth, debt reduction or a favourable definition; the quarterly term loan instalments and free cash flow provide the repayment capacity.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. First, earnings power: segment margins are very high and Scores generates a 91% operating margin, so operating income of US$1,236.3m for the last twelve months converts into analyst EBITDA of US$1,252.4m on light capital spending; the mechanism is low incremental cost, which supports debt service. Second, cash conversion: free cash flow of US$960.9m for the last twelve months and US$750.0m for nine months, supported by billing in advance, means scheduled amortisation is covered by internal cash. Third, recurring visibility in Software: annual recurring revenue of US$815.8m and net retention of 109%, with platform retention well above 100%, supports a base of contracted revenue, though it is the smaller segment. Fourth, discretionary use of cash: because the leverage increase came from repurchases, not from a structural commitment, the board can slow repurchases to reduce debt; the revolver extends to 2030 and the term loan amortises. Fifth, simple structure: the debt is unsecured, with no sponsor, and no priming, drop-down or non-pro-rata exchange is documented, though the absence of such terms in executed documents is not established.

facts.label: Conflicts and contradictions
facts.text: - Repurchase figures with different roles: the cash flow statement shows repurchases of US$3,045,992 thousand for nine months (10-Q page:4) and the stockholders' deficit statement shows US$3,052,893 thousand (10-Q page:3). The roles differ: the equity statement is on an accrual basis including excise tax and unsettled repurchases, and unsettled repurchases rose from 18,416 at September 30, 2025 to 25,318 at June 30, 2026 (10-K page:91; 10-Q page:5), a rise of 6,902 against a gap of 6,901. The handoffs use the cash figure consistently; no mismatch. Neither figure was chosen over the other by the reviewer. - Usage-based share of ACV bookings: logged in the business context as 20% in the 10-Q (page:23) and 30% in the 10-K (page:64); verified, not reconciled, immaterial to the credit view. - Presentation difference: the release condenses captions (other assets; other expense, net) relative to the 10-Q; amounts agree (release page:3, page:4; 10-Q page:2, page:3). - Correction to the credit synthesis: it states a Scores operating margin of 91% without a period. The 91% applies to the June 2026 quarter (10-Q page:32); FY2025 was 88% (10-K page:71). The synthesis conclusions do not depend on the 91% and are unchanged. The earlier handoff cannot be edited; this note is the correction. - No contradiction between modules on direction: all four describe leverage as rising, cover as falling on a run-rate basis, and liquidity as adequate near term.

facts.label: Strongest contrary evidence
facts.text: - To the claim that headroom to the covenant is thin: the ratio is 3.91x if share-based compensation is added back, which would put the ratio below the 4.0x step-down level; free cash flow of US$960.9m for the last twelve months exceeds amortisation of US$300.0m; and the board can slow repurchases. What would make it win: a covenant EBITDA definition that adds back share-based compensation or other items, or a 10-K reporting a lower ratio. The reviewer cannot resolve this without the credit agreement; the confidence of the thin-headroom claim stays Medium. - To the claim that earnings are concentrated and price dependent: Software retention of 109% and recurring revenue growth, and the nine-month text that adds mortgage volume to price as a driver. These reduce but do not remove the dependence. - To the claim that distributions are creditor-negative: the company continues to report transparently, remained in stated compliance, and has no documented creditor-adverse action; this is why the behaviour label is mechanical, not intentional.

facts.label: Downside path and monitoring triggers
facts.text: Initiating condition: a mortgage-score pricing or policy change, or a bureau pricing dispute, reduces Scores revenue per score. First operational break: segment operating income falls at a very high drop-through rate. Financial transmission: analyst EBITDA falls, which raises total debt to EBITDA from 4.46x toward the 4.5x maximum, while run-rate interest of US$316.5m is already above last twelve months cash interest of US$164.9m. Liquidity and refinancing consequence: cash of US$248.4m and a derived undrawn revolver of US$290.0m must meet US$300.0m of term loan amortisation within twelve months and, later, US$1,987.5m in FY2028. Observable triggers: the fiscal Q4 2026 release (leverage and the September 30, 2026 instalment), the pace of repurchases against free cash flow, the settlement of the accelerated share repurchase, any FHFA or bureau pricing change, and the step-down date of December 31, 2026. These triggers are monitoring items, not forecasts.

FICO's fiscal year ends September 30: fiscal Q3 2026 is the quarter ended June 30, 2026; FY2025 is the year ended September 30, 2025; "9M" is the nine months to June 30; "LTM Q3 FY2026" is the twelve months to June 30, 2026. No other currency or period is reported.

CP-0 recorded no company-defined EBITDA, no stated revolver availability and second and third quarter cash flows given year to date only. ## Findings
### Reader summary

| Operating results are strong, but debt rose to US$5,582.4m at June 30, 2026 as buybacks were debt funded. Analyst leverage reached 4.46x, close to the stated covenant ceiling. | Medium | No company EBITDA or covenant ratio is reported, and the credit agreement definitions are not supplied. |

| Revenue growth is concentrated in Scores, driven by mortgage origination score pricing. | Cash generation depends on one segment and one pricing action. | Medium |
### Financial base view

FICO's operations generate strong, growing cash flow, but the June 30, 2026 balance sheet is a different credit from the one at FY2025. In nine months, with total debt rising by US$2,526.7m, the company drew a new US$1,500.0m term loan, issued US$1,000.0m of 2034 notes, repaid the US$400.0m 2018 notes and borrowed further on the revolver, taking total debt from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m. The proceeds funded US$3,046.0m of share repurchases, including a US$1,500.0m accelerated share repurchase, far above free cash flow. On an analyst EBITDA of operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, total debt to EBITDA moved from 3.25x to 4.46x, and cash interest cover from 9.07x to 7.60x on a lagging cash-paid basis. Interest on the new debt is only partly in the last twelve months, so the run-rate burden is materially higher than reported cash interest. The main limits are the absence of a company-defined EBITDA or covenant ratio, the absence of the credit agreement, and the absence of anything after the July 29, 2026 filings. Of the term loan, US$300.0m falls due within twelve months. The base is sufficient to run the downstream modules with these limits stated.

### Quarter and post-quarter events

- Fiscal Q3 2026 financing: on "June 5, 2026, we amended our credit agreement to provide for the issuance of a $1.5 billion unsecured term loan" (10-Q page:11), and the same date an accelerated share repurchase of US$1.5bn with Wells Fargo Securities, with US$300.0m prepaid and settlement "expected to occur during the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026" (10-Q page:13).

- Fiscal Q3 2026 discrete results from the release: revenues US$674.2m, operating cash flow US$380.4m, free cash flow US$370.3m (release page:1, page:5). Interest expense, net was US$59,877 thousand against US$32,899 thousand a year earlier (10-Q page:3).
- Earlier in FY2026: US$1,000.0m of 2026 Senior Notes on March 20, 2026 and repayment of the 2018 notes on March 26, 2026 (10-Q page:12).
- Guidance (management, forward-looking): updated fiscal 2026 revenues of US$2.53 billion, GAAP net income US$850 million (release page:2).

- Subsequent events: none are listed in any source; nothing dated after July 29, 2026 is supplied, so the September 30, 2026 term loan instalment, the ASR settlement and fiscal Q4 results are Not supplied.
### Interpretation: evidence, mechanism, implication
#### Debt-funded capital return

- Evidence: total debt carrying value rose from US$3,055,691 thousand to US$5,582,389 thousand (10-K page:103; 10-Q page:10), while cash repurchases were US$3,045,992 thousand in nine months (10-Q page:4) and "Repurchases of common stock (1,706) (17) (300,000) (1,978,927)" appears in the fiscal Q3 equity statement (10-Q page:3).

- Mechanism: buybacks run at a multiple of free cash flow, so each repurchase round is financed by borrowing; the term loan was drawn for the ASR (10-Q page:22: "the proceeds of which were used to fund an accelerated share repurchase agreement").

- Credit implication: leverage is a management choice that can be reversed only by slowing repurchases or by EBITDA growth; the stockholders' deficit of US$4,097,135 thousand carries no equity cushion. Management language that the credit agreement permits repurchases (10-Q page:11) is a permission, not a commitment to deleverage.
#### Leverage against covenant

- Evidence: analyst total debt to EBITDA 4.46x at June 30, 2026 against a stated maximum "of 4.5 to 1.0 through December 30, 2026, 4.0 to 1.0 during December 31, 2026 through December 30, 2027" (10-Q page:11); "we were in compliance with all financial covenants" (10-Q page:12).

- Mechanism: the step down to 4.0x on December 31, 2026 and 3.5x on December 31, 2027 shrinks permitted leverage unless EBITDA grows or debt is repaid; the term loan amortises US$75.0m a quarter. The covenant definition is not supplied, so the analyst ratio is context, not a test.

- Credit implication: on a measure that adds back share-based compensation the ratio is 3.91x; on the plain measure it is 4.46x. Headroom is Not calculable until the credit agreement definition is obtained; the range indicates headroom is thin to moderate before the first step down.
#### Interest burden

- Evidence: last twelve months cash interest US$164,872 thousand; contractual annualised interest on June 30, 2026 balances is US$316,510 thousand (Calculations). Interest expense, net for nine months rose to US$146,462 thousand from US$93,765 thousand (10-Q page:3).

- Mechanism: the term loan was drawn on June 5, 2026 and the 2026 notes on March 20, 2026, so only weeks to months of their interest are in the twelve-month figures; the term loan and revolver float over SOFR (10-Q page:41).
- Credit implication: forward cover is closer to 3.96x than 7.60x on unchanged EBITDA; floating-rate exposure applies to US$2,210.0m of borrowings (revolver plus term loan).
#### Revenue concentration in Scores

- Evidence: Scores revenue was US$458,897 thousand of US$674,188 thousand in fiscal Q3 2026 (10-Q page:2), and "The increase in business-to-business scores revenue was primarily attributable to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price" (10-Q page:26). Software revenue rose 2% in the quarter (10-Q page:25).
- Mechanism: earnings growth rests on pricing in one product line sold through credit reporting agencies and exposed to mortgage volumes and the antitrust claim (10-Q page:43).
- Credit implication: cash flow quality is high today but price-dependent; a pricing reversal would hit EBITDA and the covenant ratio at once.
## Calculations
All inputs are US$ thousands as printed unless marked.
### LTM construction

### EBITDA, leverage and cover
- Face-value basis: the face total at June 30, 2026 is 710,000 + 1,500,000 + 3,400,000 = 5,610,000; 5,610,000 / 1,252,442 = 4.48x. The carrying basis is used in the charts.

EBITDA / annualised interest = 1,252,442 / 316,510 = 3.96x. Excludes credit agreement fees, issuance cost amortisation and interest income; rates are the weighted or stated June 30, 2026 rates and float.
### Liquidity and maturities

- Term loan schedule: instalments of 75,000 on September 30, 2026, December 31, 2026, March 31, 2027 and June 30, 2027 (300,000, matching "$300.0 million principal payments due on our term loan over the next 12 months", 10-Q page:33) then 112,500 on September 30, 2027, December 31, 2027 and March 31, 2028 (337,500), leaving 1,500,000 - 300,000 - 337,500 = 862,500 at May 15, 2028. By fiscal year: FY2026 75,000; FY2027 225,000 + 112,500 = 337,500; FY2028 225,000 + 862,500 = 1,087,500 plus notes 900,000 = 1,987,500. Sum of all rows: 75,000 + 337,500 + 1,987,500 + 710,000 + 1,500,000 + 1,000,000 = 5,610,000.
- Buybacks less free cash flow, nine months FY2026: 3,045,992 - 750,034 = 2,295,958.
### Free cash flow and reconciliations

- Free cash flow = operating cash flow - (purchases of property and equipment + capitalised internal-use software). 9M FY2026: 777,880 - (1,355 + 26,491) = 750,034, against 750,035 printed by the release (release page:5), a rounding difference of 1. 9M FY2025: 555,138 - (4,751 + 21,831) = 528,556, equal to the release. FY2025: 778,807 - (8,922 + 30,485) = 739,400. FY2024: 632,964 - (8,884 + 16,667) = 607,413.

- Income statement block, 9M FY2026: revenues 1,877,824 - total operating expenses 878,682 = 999,142 operating income (10-Q page:2, page:3); FY2025: 1,990,869 - 1,066,019 = 924,850 (10-K page:89). Debt table: 300,000 + 5,282,389 = 5,582,389.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| FICO is a profitable, asset-light scoring and software business whose revenue leans on three credit bureaus and mortgage score pricing. It is a public company with no sponsor that now funds large buybacks with debt. | Medium | Ownership, proxy governance and executed financing documents are not supplied. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Three consumer reporting agencies produced 63% of revenue in the June 2026 quarter, up from 54% a year earlier. | Revenue is concentrated in a few counterparties whose pricing practices can affect FICO. | High |

| Scores revenue growth in the quarter was primarily attributed to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price. | Earnings growth depends on pricing that regulators or the bureaus could change. | Medium |

| The 2026 financing events were a new term loan, new 2034 notes and an accelerated share repurchase, with the term loan proceeds used for the repurchase. | Debt-funded shareholder returns lower the cushion for creditors. | High |
| Software recurring revenue is shifting to the platform product while non-platform recurring revenue declines. | Software growth is modest and does not offset Scores dependence. | Medium |
| An antitrust class action over FICO Score distribution continues, with no amount or accrual stated. | A contingent claim exists without any quantified exposure. | Low |
### Business and transaction view

FICO is a Delaware-incorporated, NYSE-listed analytics company with two segments. Scores sells the FICO Score mainly through Experian, TransUnion and Equifax, which pay FICO a fee for each score generated; Software sells decisioning products as SaaS or on-premises. Revenue is concentrated by counterparty (three bureaus), by end market (financial services) and by geography (the Americas), and recent growth is concentrated in Scores pricing on mortgage originations. The company has no sponsor and no controlling holder is evidenced in the supplied sources; ownership detail sits in a proxy statement that is not supplied. The creditor-relevant change in the period is financial policy: in FY2026 the company issued new notes, drew a term loan and funded a large accelerated share repurchase, taking analyst total debt to EBITDA to 4.46x per the financial base. The documented behaviour is debt-funded shareholder distribution within the permissions of an unsecured credit agreement and in compliance with its stated covenants; no priming, drop-down or non-pro-rata exchange is documented. The business is high-margin and cash generative, but its revenue depends on a small number of counterparties and on score pricing, so the credit rests on continued pricing power and on management's leverage choices, not on structural protection.
### Company and operating model
| Driver | What the source says | Evidence (locator) | Risk mechanic | Creditor implication | Category |

| Scores B2B revenue model | Scores are sold through consumer reporting agencies, which pay FICO a fee for each score generated | 10-K page:6: "Users of our scores generally pay the consumer reporting agencies a fee for each individual score generated by our algorithms, and the consumer reporting agencies pay an associated fee to us" | Revenue is per-score volume times a unit price set in bureau contracts; FICO does not hold the credit data or sell directly to most lenders | Volume (originations, applications) and price are the two drivers of the largest profit pool; the bureaus are intermediaries and customers | Documentary Fact |

| Bureau concentration | Experian, TransUnion and Equifax each exceed 10% of revenue | 10-Q page:15: "accounted for 63% and 54% of our total revenues in the quarters ended June 30, 2026 and 2025" | Loss, repricing or distribution change at one bureau hits a large share of revenue | Counterparty concentration raises revenue volatility; bureaus also compete with FICO scores | Documentary Fact |

| Mortgage pricing | B2B growth tied to mortgage origination score price | 10-Q page:26: "primarily attributable to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price" | Price actions on a regulated, mortgage-linked product drive margin; FHFA rules can change the score used | Growth of this size is not repeatable by volume alone and is exposed to policy change | Documentary Fact |

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

There is no sponsor transaction, merger or acquisition in the supplied sources; the context lists no deal terms. The transactions that matter to a creditor are the issuer's own financing and capital return events in fiscal 2026. On March 20, 2026 the company issued senior notes carrying a 6.25% coupon and maturing September 15, 2034, in a private offering to qualified institutional investors, and on March 26, 2026 it used the proceeds to repay in full the 2018 Senior Notes before their May 2026 maturity (10-Q page:12). - Usage-based share of ACV bookings: the 10-Q states "ACV Bookings related to estimates of future usage-based fees was approximately 20% of the total ACV Bookings amount on an annualized basis" (10-Q page:23), while the 10-K states "approximately 30% of the total ACV Bookings amount on an annualized basis" (10-K page:64). The periods differ; both are logged and neither is chosen or reconciled. Effect: usage-based exposure of recurring software bookings is Not determinable as a single figure.
- No other conflict between filings and releases was found in the lines read.
### Credit translations
#### Revenue durability

- Evidence: bureau revenue was 63% of the June 2026 quarter (10-Q page:15) and the Scores segment growth was "primarily attributable to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price" (10-Q page:26).
- Mechanic: a per-score fee through three intermediaries means a small number of contract terms and one pricing lever set revenue; Software is a smaller, slower segment.

- Implication: revenue is durable while FICO Score use is required or preferred in mortgage and consumer credit decisions, but pricing and policy shifts can lower it quickly; a revenue shortfall hits debt service and the covenant ratio together. Counter: the retention rate above 100% in platform software (10-Q page:25) supports part of the base.
#### Margin and cash-flow risk
- Evidence: Scores operating margin of 91% (10-Q page:32) and free cash flow of US$750.0m for nine months (CP-1).
- Mechanic: high operating leverage means revenue changes flow almost fully to EBITDA; cash conversion is high because capital spending is light.
- Implication: cash flow could service the new debt if price and volume hold, but the interest run-rate is far above LTM cash interest per CP-1, so margin of safety depends on revenue holding.
#### Concentration and policy risk
- Evidence: bureau concentration (10-Q page:15), financial services 92% and Americas 87% of FY2025 revenue (10-K page:15), and FHFA policy exposure (10-K page:36).
- Mechanic: single-counterparty, single-sector and single-policy exposures are correlated with the mortgage cycle.
- Implication: tail risk of loss of score preference, not covered by diversification.
#### Sponsor alignment and financial policy
- Evidence: no sponsor; debt-funded repurchases with a $2.0 billion authorisation (10-Q page:36).
- Mechanic: shareholder-return policy sets leverage; the board can reverse it, but nothing in the supplied documents commits it to a leverage target.

- Implication: leverage tolerance is a management and board choice; creditors rely on covenants (4.5x stepping to 4.0x on December 31, 2026) not on sponsor support. Monitoring: watch repurchase pace against free cash flow and the covenant step-downs.
#### Key uncertainties
- Ownership and board detail (proxy), executed financing documents, the status of FHFA policy after July 2025, the antitrust case outcome, and all events after July 29, 2026 are Not supplied.

## Calculations

None new. CP-1A calculates nothing. Figures are quoted source labels or references to accepted CP-1 figures: total debt US$3,055.7m and US$5,582.4m, analyst total debt to EBITDA 4.46x, cash US$248.4m, derived undrawn revolver US$290.0m, free cash flow US$750.0m and cash repurchases US$3,046.0m for nine months, amortisation of US$300.0m within twelve months. ## Request
- Issuer: FAIR ISAAC CORP (Fair Isaac Corporation, NYSE "FICO", issuer id `fico`), as of 2026-11-05, information cutoff 2026-11-05.

- Scope: the fundamental credit view a committee reads first, synthesised from the settled upstream registers only: business risk from the business and transaction context, financial risk and liquidity from the financial base, and the gaps that limit both. Creditor perspective.
- Prohibited and not done: no peer ranking, no instrument recommendation, no recovery conclusion. Recovery appears only as a mechanic where relevant. No rating is assigned.

- Evidence rule: upstream only. This module re-read no source text and quotes nothing. Every row names its basis: rows of the business context register (ids F1 to F21, in Basis columns only) or CP-1 figures. Figures are CP-1 figures as written there.
- Periods and currency: USD; fiscal year ends September 30; fiscal Q3 2026 is the quarter ended June 30, 2026; LTM Q3 FY2026 is the twelve months to June 30, 2026.

- Inherited limitations (carried, not restated as findings): from CP-0 and CP-1, no company-defined EBITDA or covenant ratio, no executed financing documents, undrawn revolver derived without letters of credit, and no evidence dated after July 29, 2026. From the business context, the proxy statement is not supplied and the readiness judgment of this module is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS, so confidence is below High.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| FICO has strong, cash-generative earnings, but debt-funded buybacks lifted analyst leverage to 4.46x against a covenant maximum of 4.5x that steps down. The credit depends on pricing and on shareholder-return choices. | Medium | The covenant definition and executed financing documents are not supplied, so headroom cannot be measured. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |
| Total debt rose from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m in nine months because buybacks exceeded free cash flow. | Leverage is a policy choice and can rise again. | High |
| Analyst EBITDA gives a cushion of only 0.95% below the 4.5x covenant maximum at June 30, 2026. | Little room before the step down to 4.0x on December 31, 2026. | Medium |
| Annualised contractual interest is US$316.5m against last twelve months cash interest of US$164.9m. | Cover falls to 3.96x on the run-rate from 7.60x as reported. | Medium |
| Bureau concentration and mortgage pricing drive earnings. | A pricing or policy change would cut EBITDA and leverage headroom together. | Medium |
| Free cash flow of US$960.9m for the last twelve months exceeds the US$300.0m of term loan amortisation due within twelve months. | Scheduled debt service is covered if earnings hold. | Medium |
### Credit view

FICO's business risk is strong on earnings quality but narrow on sources: a per-score fee model with very high segment margins, recurring Software revenue with net retention above 100%, light capital spending and consistent free cash flow. Its financial risk has moved sharply in fiscal 2026. Total debt rose from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m while cash repurchases of US$3,046.0m for nine months far exceeded free cash flow of US$750.0m, and analyst total debt to EBITDA rose from 3.25x at FY2025 to 4.46x at June 30, 2026, which is 4.26x net. The stated covenant maximum is 4.5x until December 30, 2026, then 4.0x, then 3.5x, and on the analyst measure the cushion below 4.5x is thin; on a sensitivity that adds back share-based compensation the ratio is 3.91x. The covenant definition is not supplied, so headroom is Not calculable. Interest on the June 2026 debt is only partly in reported cash interest, so run-rate cover is about 3.96x against 7.60x reported. Liquidity is adequate for the near term but not generous: cash of US$248.4m plus a derived undrawn revolver of US$290.0m, against US$300.0m of term loan amortisation due within twelve months, which free cash flow comfortably covers. The next refinancing step is large: US$1,987.5m falls due in FY2028, when the term loan balance and the 2019 and 2021 notes mature. Because the debt is unsecured and no creditor-adverse action is documented, the creditor relies on covenants, cash generation and the board's financial policy, not on collateral or a sponsor. Overall the fundamental credit view is a high-quality earnings stream carrying a materially higher and still discretionary debt load; confidence is medium because covenant definitions, ownership detail and everything after July 29, 2026 are Not supplied.
### Key findings

The most important finding is that leverage is now set by shareholder-return policy rather than by operations. CP-1 shows total debt up from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m over nine months and nine-month cash repurchases of US$3,046.0m against free cash flow of US$750.0m; the business context shows the term loan proceeds were used to fund an accelerated share repurchase and that a $2.0 billion repurchase authorisation is in place. The mechanism is direct: each repurchase round is financed by borrowing, so analyst total debt to EBITDA of 4.46x can rise or fall by board decision alone. The implication is that the creditor's leverage tolerance depends on a choice nobody has committed to constrain, other than the financial covenant.

The second finding is the covenant path. The stated maximum consolidated leverage ratio is 4.5x until December 30, 2026, 4.0x from December 31, 2026 and 3.5x from December 31, 2027. On the analyst measure of operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, total debt to EBITDA is 4.46x, which leaves a cushion of 0.95% of EBITDA below 4.5x (Calculations); on the sensitivity with share-based compensation added back it is 3.91x. The covenant definition is not supplied, so neither is the covenant ratio, and the compliance statement in the filings is the only evidence of headroom. The step down to 4.0x on December 31, 2026 requires EBITDA growth, debt reduction or a favourable definition; the quarterly term loan instalments and free cash flow provide the repayment capacity.

The third finding is interest burden. Cash interest paid in the last twelve months is US$164.9m but annualised contractual interest on June 30, 2026 balances is US$316.5m, because the term loan was drawn on June 5, 2026 and the 2026 notes in March 2026. Cover is 7.60x as reported and 3.96x on the run-rate. About US$2,210.0m of borrowings float over SOFR, so base rates feed straight into the burden.

The fourth finding is revenue concentration. Three consumer reporting agencies produced 63% of revenue in the June 2026 quarter, and Scores growth was primarily attributed to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price. The mechanism is that a per-score fee through three intermediaries, a regulated mortgage channel and a single price lever determine most of earnings and almost all of the incremental margin, given a Scores margin of 91%. A pricing, volume or policy change therefore hits EBITDA, interest cover and covenant headroom together.

The fifth finding is liquidity and maturities. Cash is US$248.4m, the derived undrawn revolver is US$290.0m before letters of credit, and US$300.0m of term loan amortisation falls due within twelve months, against last twelve months free cash flow of US$960.9m. The maturity profile is back-ended into FY2028, when US$1,987.5m falls due. The implication is that near-term liquidity is sufficient but refinancing will need market access at higher coupons, since the 2026 notes carry 6.25% against 5.25% on the repaid notes.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. First, earnings power: segment margins are very high and Scores generates a 91% operating margin, so operating income of US$1,236.3m for the last twelve months converts into analyst EBITDA of US$1,252.4m on light capital spending; the mechanism is low incremental cost, which supports debt service. Second, cash conversion: free cash flow of US$960.9m for the last twelve months and US$750.0m for nine months, supported by billing in advance, means scheduled amortisation is covered by internal cash. Third, recurring visibility in Software: annual recurring revenue of US$815.8m and net retention of 109%, with platform retention well above 100%, supports a base of contracted revenue, though it is the smaller segment. Fourth, discretionary use of cash: because the leverage increase came from repurchases, not from a structural commitment, the board can slow repurchases to reduce debt; the revolver extends to 2030 and the term loan amortises. Fifth, simple structure: the debt is unsecured, with no sponsor, and no priming, drop-down or non-pro-rata exchange is documented, though the absence of such terms in executed documents is not established.

Weaknesses. First, leverage and covenant path: 4.46x on the analyst measure against a 4.5x maximum that steps to 4.0x and 3.5x; the mechanism is shrinking permitted leverage unless EBITDA grows or debt is repaid. Second, financial policy: debt-funded distributions of US$3,046.0m for nine months against free cash flow of US$750.0m, with a stockholders' deficit that carries no equity cushion. Third, concentration: bureaus at 63% of revenue, financial services at 92% and the Americas at 87% of FY2025 revenue, and mortgage-policy exposure. Fourth, interest burden: run-rate interest of US$316.5m is nearly double last twelve months cash interest, with floating-rate exposure. Fifth, disclosure limits: no company EBITDA, no covenant ratio, no executed documents, no proxy statement, no data after July 29, 2026; these restrict monitoring more than they signal risk, and missing evidence is not treated as adverse.
### Credit assessment
| Dimension | Assessment | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Business risk | Strong earnings quality, narrow sources: three bureaus, one price lever, mortgage-linked | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | F1, F3, F4, F16, the operating model rows on mortgage pricing and policy, and CP-1 free cash flow |

| Financial risk | Elevated and rising: total debt to EBITDA 4.46x, cover 7.60x reported and 3.96x run-rate | Documentary Fact for the figures; Analyst Interpretation for the reading | Medium | CP-1 leverage and cover figures |

| Liquidity | Adequate near term, thin surplus: cash US$248.4m, derived undrawn revolver US$290.0m, US$300.0m amortisation within twelve months | Documentary Fact and derived figure | Medium | CP-1 liquidity and maturity figures |
| Governance and financial policy | Shareholder-return led; debt-funded repurchases; no creditor-adverse action documented | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | F11, F12, F13, F19 |

| Overall fundamental credit view | A high-quality earnings stream with a materially higher, discretionary debt load; headroom to the covenant is thin on the analyst measure | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | All of the above |

Thesis (one sentence): FICO's very profitable, cash-generative but concentrated Scores franchise supports its debt, while debt-funded buybacks and a stepping-down leverage covenant make the credit depend on pricing power and on the board's financial policy.
### Strengths and weaknesses register
| Item | Type | Text | Category | Basis |
| S1 | Strength | High margins and cash conversion: free cash flow US$960.9m for the last twelve months | Documentary Fact | CP-1 free cash flow; operating model rows on Scores margin |
| S2 | Strength | Recurring Software visibility: annual recurring revenue and net retention above 100% overall | Documentary Fact | Business context operating model rows |
| S3 | Strength | Discretionary buybacks allow deleveraging by decision; revolver runs to 2030 | Analyst Interpretation | F11, F12; CP-1 maturities |
| S4 | Strength | Unsecured structure, no sponsor and no documented creditor-adverse action | Insufficient Information on executed terms | F8, F20 |
| W1 | Weakness | Leverage 4.46x against 4.5x maximum stepping to 4.0x and 3.5x | Documentary Fact for the figures | CP-1 leverage; F19 |
| W2 | Weakness | Debt-funded distributions exceeding free cash flow; stockholders' deficit | Documentary Fact | CP-1 financial base; F13 |
| W3 | Weakness | Bureau, sector, geographic and mortgage-policy concentration | Documentary Fact | F3, F4 and the operating model rows on mortgage pricing and policy |
| W4 | Weakness | Run-rate interest US$316.5m against LTM cash interest US$164.9m; floating-rate borrowings | Documentary Fact for the figures | CP-1 interest figures |
| W5 | Weakness | Missing covenant definition, executed documents, proxy and later events | Insufficient Information | F8, F10, F21 |
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity | Basis |

| Covenant step-down against rising leverage | Maximum falls to 4.0x on December 31, 2026 and 3.5x on December 31, 2027 while analyst leverage is 4.46x | Possible covenant pressure or forced slowing of buybacks; amendment cost; headroom Not calculable | Material | CP-1 leverage; F19 |

| Debt-funded shareholder returns | Repurchases financed by term loan and notes; authorisation of $2.0 billion | Leverage tolerance set by the board; renewed borrowing could reverse deleveraging | Material | F11, F12, F13; CP-1 financial base |

| Revenue concentration and pricing dependence | Three bureaus at 63% of the June 2026 quarter; Scores growth attributed to unit price | Earnings and covenant headroom fall together if price or policy changes | Material | F3, F4 and the operating model rows on mortgage pricing and policy |

| Interest burden step-up and floating rate | Run-rate interest US$316.5m; term loan and revolver float over SOFR | Cover falls to 3.96x on run-rate; rates feed through | Material | CP-1 interest figures |
| FY2028 refinancing | US$1,987.5m falls due in FY2028 | Needs market access at higher coupons than the repaid notes | Material | CP-1 maturities chart |
| Antitrust litigation | Class action over FICO Score distribution continues; no amount stated | Contingent claim not quantified | Minor | F16, F17 |
| Information gaps | No covenant definition, proxy, executed documents or post-July 2026 evidence | Restricts monitoring; not an adverse conclusion | Minor | F8, F10, F21 |
## Calculations
All inputs are CP-1 figures in US$ thousands as written there. These are new calculations in this module.

- EBITDA needed at the 4.5x covenant maximum on the analyst construction: 5,582,389 / 4.5 = 1,240,531. LTM Q3 FY2026 analyst EBITDA is 1,252,442. Difference 1,252,442 - 1,240,531 = 11,911, which is 0.95% of 1,252,442. This is the cushion under the analyst measure, not a covenant headroom.

- EBITDA needed at 4.0x at the same debt: 5,582,389 / 4.0 = 1,395,597; shortfall against 1,252,442 is 143,155. On the sensitivity with share-based compensation added back, EBITDA is 1,426,731, which exceeds 1,395,597, so the ratio is 3.91x (5,582,389 / 1,426,731). Neither is the covenant calculation; the definition is not supplied.
- Free cash flow against amortisation: LTM free cash flow 960,878 exceeds the 300,000 term loan principal due within twelve months (CP-1; the loan schedule is derived from 10-Q summary terms).
- Floating-rate borrowings: 710,000 + 1,500,000 = 2,210,000 (revolver plus term loan, CP-1 debt table).

- No other new figures. All other values are CP-1 figures as written: total debt 3,055,691 and 5,582,389; cash repurchases 3,045,992 and free cash flow 750,034 for nine months; cash interest 164,872; annualised interest 316,510; cover 7.60x and 3.96x; leverage 3.25x, 4.46x, 4.26x and 3.91x.
## Gaps
| Gap | Why it matters | Affects | Severity | Action |

| Credit agreement, June 5, 2026 amendment and covenant definitions not supplied; reported leverage ratio not printed | Headroom to the maximum leverage ratio cannot be measured | Financial risk, covenant risk | Material | Obtain the executed documents; until then headroom is Not calculable |

| Indentures, guarantor structure and repurchase agreement terms not supplied | Distribution capacity and any guarantees cannot be verified | Governance, creditor control | Material | Obtain; guarantors Not supplied |
| 2026 Proxy Statement not supplied | Ownership, board and related-party dealings unknown | Governance, willingness | Medium | Obtain the proxy |

| Nothing after July 29, 2026: September 30, 2026 instalment, ASR settlement, fiscal Q4 and FY2026 results | Leverage and liquidity at the fiscal year end are unknown | All | Material | Add later filings |
| Letters of credit usage not disclosed | Undrawn revolver of US$290.0m is an upper bound | Liquidity | Medium | Obtain disclosure |
| FHFA policy status after July 2025 not updated in the 10-Qs | Mortgage score preference could change | Business risk | Medium | Monitor |
| Antitrust case outcome and exposure unknown | Contingent claim not quantified | Contingent claims | Minor | Monitor |
| Usage-based ACV share differs between filings (logged, not reconciled) | Software visibility slightly uncertain | Business risk | Minor | Note only |
## Next module

Run CP-5 next on this module with CP-1 and CP-1A. Review in particular: the cushion figure under the 4.5x covenant maximum, which is an analyst construction; the run-rate interest and cover figures; the derived undrawn revolver and maturity schedule; and the statements about creditor-adverse actions, which rest on the filings read and not on executed documents.

The trace holds. All 29 quotations in the financial base and business context handoffs were found, and each sits on the page it cites. In the readiness handoff every quotation of source text was found; its three other quoted strings are search terms or paraphrases, not source quotations. Every non-derived figure in those handoffs appears in the pinned sources, and every derived figure recomputes from its cited inputs. Second, statements about the absence of creditor-adverse terms and about covenant headroom are absence-of-evidence claims and are bounded by the missing credit agreement, indentures and proxy. ### Conflicts and contradictions

- Repurchase figures with different roles: the cash flow statement shows repurchases of US$3,045,992 thousand for nine months (10-Q page:4) and the stockholders' deficit statement shows US$3,052,893 thousand (10-Q page:3). The roles differ: the equity statement is on an accrual basis including excise tax and unsettled repurchases, and unsettled repurchases rose from 18,416 at September 30, 2025 to 25,318 at June 30, 2026 (10-K page:91; 10-Q page:5), a rise of 6,902 against a gap of 6,901. The handoffs use the cash figure consistently; no mismatch. Neither figure was chosen over the other by the reviewer.
- Usage-based share of ACV bookings: logged in the business context as 20% in the 10-Q (page:23) and 30% in the 10-K (page:64); verified, not reconciled, immaterial to the credit view.
- Presentation difference: the release condenses captions (other assets; other expense, net) relative to the 10-Q; amounts agree (release page:3, page:4; 10-Q page:2, page:3).

- Correction to the credit synthesis: it states a Scores operating margin of 91% without a period. The 91% applies to the June 2026 quarter (10-Q page:32); FY2025 was 88% (10-K page:71). The synthesis conclusions do not depend on the 91% and are unchanged. The earlier handoff cannot be edited; this note is the correction.
- No contradiction between modules on direction: all four describe leverage as rising, cover as falling on a run-rate basis, and liquidity as adequate near term.
### Research integrity grade and committee use

Committee status: Restricted. Quality grade: the evidence trace is clean; the restriction arises from missing documents and the analyst-constructed nature of the covenant-related metrics, not from defects in the trace. Confidence band: Low under the Restricted cap; no numeric score is asserted by the reviewer.

| Guarantor, security, priming or distribution restriction conclusions | No | Indentures and credit agreement not supplied |

### Strongest contrary evidence

- To the claim that headroom to the covenant is thin: the ratio is 3.91x if share-based compensation is added back, which would put the ratio below the 4.0x step-down level; free cash flow of US$960.9m for the last twelve months exceeds amortisation of US$300.0m; and the board can slow repurchases. What would make it win: a covenant EBITDA definition that adds back share-based compensation or other items, or a 10-K reporting a lower ratio. The reviewer cannot resolve this without the credit agreement; the confidence of the thin-headroom claim stays Medium.

- To the claim that earnings are concentrated and price dependent: Software retention of 109% and recurring revenue growth, and the nine-month text that adds mortgage volume to price as a driver. These reduce but do not remove the dependence.

- To the claim that distributions are creditor-negative: the company continues to report transparently, remained in stated compliance, and has no documented creditor-adverse action; this is why the behaviour label is mechanical, not intentional.
### Downside path and monitoring triggers

Initiating condition: a mortgage-score pricing or policy change, or a bureau pricing dispute, reduces Scores revenue per score. First operational break: segment operating income falls at a very high drop-through rate. Financial transmission: analyst EBITDA falls, which raises total debt to EBITDA from 4.46x toward the 4.5x maximum, while run-rate interest of US$316.5m is already above last twelve months cash interest of US$164.9m. Liquidity and refinancing consequence: cash of US$248.4m and a derived undrawn revolver of US$290.0m must meet US$300.0m of term loan amortisation within twelve months and, later, US$1,987.5m in FY2028. Observable triggers: the fiscal Q4 2026 release (leverage and the September 30, 2026 instalment), the pace of repurchases against free cash flow, the settlement of the accelerated share repurchase, any FHFA or bureau pricing change, and the step-down date of December 31, 2026. These triggers are monitoring items, not forecasts.

| Credit agreement, June 5, 2026 amendment, indentures and ASR agreement not supplied | Material | Covenant, guarantor, security and distribution conclusions | Obtain executed documents; keep Restricted until then |

| Reviewer did not inspect images, charts or XBRL; tables were read from text extraction | Low | Table fidelity | Spot-check against filed HTML |
| Credit synthesis margin wording | Minor | Wording only | Corrected in this handoff |
## Next module

This is the last module of the minimum set.
